pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 56. Bowls sold: 30. Stories told: 1. Ama's mood: talking.*

Sunday was the worst day to be awake. The sun was too bright, and the apartment was too quiet. I sat at the small wooden table, my dark green jacket still on, my shoes still laced. My feet hung over the edge of the chair, toes tapping a rhythm I did not choose.

The balcony door creaked. Ama stood there, her silver curls slightly mussed, her right wrist wrapped in a white brace. She had been out there since dawn, sitting on the little plastic stool with her knees drawn up. The air smelled of cold concrete and old tea.

She looked at me, then at the notebook open on the table. The pages were blank. I had not written a single number.

"Come," she said, her voice rough from the dry air. "Bring your notebook."

I shook my head. My throat felt tight. "I do not want to write anything down, Ama. I do not want to measure your soup. I just want it to stop."

Ama stepped over the threshold. She did not look angry. She looked tired, the way the market looks at eleven p.m. when the last stool is being tucked under the table.

"Bring it anyway," she said.
pages.image: Ama, a small sturdy grandmother with short silver curls and a flowery padded vest, her right wrist in a white brace, stands beside a wooden table in a dim small apartment while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, sits stiffly at the table.

pages.text:
Ama pulled out a plastic stool and sat down. She did not sit across from me. She sat beside me, close enough that I could feel the warmth of her shoulder. She began to speak, and her words came out in a slow, low mix of Mandarin and the Hokkien she used with Ba. I had to lean forward, my chin in my hands, just to catch the sounds.

"When I was eleven," she said, "my mother had a cart. It was not a stall. It was a cart with four wheels and a tarp that smelled of rain." She paused, her left hand rubbing the edge of the table. "She sold pork bone soup. Beef was too expensive. We had no money for beef."

I looked at her. I could not remember ever asking about before the stall.

"I hated the cart," Ama said. Her eyes were fixed on a spot on the floor. "When the girls from school walked by, I hid behind the stove. I pretended I did not know her. I thought if I did not look at it, it would not be me." She turned to me, her square face serious. "You know what that is, Lin? It is the same feeling you have now. It is not about the smell. It is about being seen."
pages.image: Ama with short silver curls sits on a plastic stool beside Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, both looking down at a wooden table in a sunlit room, Ama serious and reflective.

pages.text:
"My mother did not have a recipe," Ama continued, her voice steady. "She had a feeling. When winter came and the whole lane caught colds, she put in more ginger. When summer came and sugar cost too much, she used less. The broth changed every year. It was never the same soup two winters running."

She reached out and tapped the table with one finger, making a soft knock that sounded like a pencil on a desk.

"When Agong's factory closed, I opened Stall 19. People asked for beef, so I used beef. But the method was hers. There is no recipe, Lin. There is only a river."

Her voice dropped, almost to a whisper, as if she were sharing a secret about a forbidden snack.

"My mother stepped in first. I stepped in second. Somebody has to step in third. The water will not look the same, and that is how you know it is still running. A river that does not move is a pond. And ponds get stagnant."
pages.image: Ama, with short silver curls and a flowery vest, gestures with one hand as she talks to Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, who listens intently with hands clasped, in a simple sunlit room.

pages.text:
I swallowed, the taste of salt rising in my throat. "Nobody told me that. Nobody told me it was supposed to change. I thought it was broken because I couldn't copy it."

Ama shook her head slowly. She lifted her right hand, the one in the brace, and held it up in the light. It trembled, a small, quiet shake like a leaf caught in a draft.

"My hand is not what it was," she said. "It will heal, but it will not be the same. I am afraid that the stall will not survive me. I am afraid that if you change it, if you add your own thing, it will stop being mine."

She looked at me, her eyes bright and wet.

"I was wrong. A thing that cannot change is a thing already gone. I was trying to keep it safe. I should have been trying to keep it alive."
pages.image: Ama with short silver curls holds up her right hand in a white brace while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, looks at her with shock and realization, warm quiet sunlit room.

pages.text:
I looked down at the notebook. The pencil behind my ear felt heavy. For weeks, I had reached for it without thinking. Now, I did not want to measure. I did not want to count. I just wanted to sit there.

"I am sorry," I said. The words felt small in the big room. "I am sorry I thought it was embarrassing. I am sorry I ran to the temple."

Ama reached over and took my hand. Her fingers were rough and strong, even with the brace. "I am sorry too," she said. "I am sorry I made you carry it all by yourself."

We sat there in the noon light. The smell of star anise and ginger hung in the air, thick and warm. It did not smell like soup. It smelled like us. Then, very quietly, Ama began to hum. It was that old song with no words. I listened, and I let the sound fill the room.
pages.image: Ama in her flowery vest sits close to Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, their hands touching on a wooden table, both peaceful, in a sunlit room full of warmth.
